metadata.title: Mental Wellbeing Community Platform Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a wellbeing community would need to change when recommendations face clinical-style oversight, an employer asks for private member signals, a regional crisis overwhelms available support, or all three pressures arrive together.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A member signs in through an employer or personal account, describes a need, receives recommended content, communities, live sessions, or referrals, participates, and generates engagement data that appears in employer reporting. The design assumes recommendations remain an unregulated product feature, employers accept aggregate reporting, and suitable support remains available when a member needs it.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates private member identity and activity from employer eligibility and reporting; records why a support option was shown, which policy and scope allowed it, and when a human reviewed it; and models member need, urgency, consent, location, support type, provider capacity, referral, and follow-up independently. This lets the platform explain recommendations without presenting them as diagnosis, refuse inappropriate employer access, and route a demand surge through safe community support and external care options.
metadata.note: These tests start with regulation, customer power, and a community-wide capacity shock. They test the business and operating model, not only whether an app or database stays online. The platform provides peer and wellbeing support; it must not silently turn recommendations into diagnosis or treatment.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: A regulator treats automated wellbeing recommendations like regulated clinical decisions
stressors.detection: Final regulatory guidance, legal interpretation, enforcement notices, product classification decisions, recommendation complaints, contributor feedback, and audits of what the platform claims and records.
stressors.attractor: A convenient recommendation feed is interpreted as making consequential health decisions without enough explanation, evidence, role boundaries, or human oversight. Disabling all personalization protects compliance but makes timely support harder to find; leaving it unchanged threatens trust and market access.
stressors.businessReaction: State clearly what the platform does and does not provide, classify each support pathway, document why an option was offered, require human review for defined cases, preserve an appeal and correction route, and redirect clinical needs to qualified services without claiming to diagnose the member.
stressors.residue: Separate the member's expressed intent from inferred need, recommendation candidate, contributor scope, content classification, policy version, decision evidence, explanation, human review, and referral outcome. A recommendation may only use approved evidence and scope; higher-consequence paths stop for human review or present an external care route rather than a diagnosis.

impacts.effect: Fast support discovery now includes a visible boundary between peer wellbeing support, guided referral, and clinical care.
Members can understand why an option fits, what it can help with, and when qualified care is the safer next step.
Trust and fit include recommendation evidence, contributor scope, limitations, human review, and a correction or appeal path.
Safety incidents are traced to the policy, evidence, recommendation, review, and follow-up that shaped the member path.
Adds understandable recommendation explanations, scope labels, review states, consent prompts, and safe referral choices.
Makes fast discovery conditional on approved support scope and sends consequential cases through a reviewable path.
Stores candidates, evidence, policy version, explanation, decision, and review rather than only a ranked result.
Evaluates models against permitted purpose, explainability, drift, safety boundaries, and human-review rules.
Owns the handoff from automated discovery to trained human review and documented escalation.
Owns recommendation policy and evidence with member, clinical-safety, legal, contributor, and care-navigation partners.
Makes explainable personalization and clear care boundaries part of the trusted digital-wellbeing benchmark.

stressors.name: A major employer demands named employee wellbeing-risk scores and intervention lists
stressors.detection: Procurement requirements, executive requests, renewal negotiations, admin support tickets, proposed data exports, privacy reviews, member research, and workforce or union concerns.
stressors.attractor: The buyer funds access and expects actionable workforce intelligence, but fulfilling the request would turn confidential member activity into an employment signal. Refusing without an alternative puts the contract at risk; complying undermines member safety, participation, and the platform's promise.
stressors.businessReaction: Refuse individual surveillance, restate the permitted purpose of employer reporting, offer privacy-protected aggregate program signals and voluntary support campaigns, apply minimum cohort and suppression rules, and make every employer query and export auditable.
stressors.residue: Separate employer, benefit contract, eligibility record, member account, consent, private activity, program cohort, aggregate measure, suppression decision, admin role, query, and export. Employer views operate only on approved cohort aggregates; private activity cannot be joined back to a worker unless a separately governed, explicit emergency or legal process applies.

impacts.effect: Employer value is proven through responsible program outcomes, not visibility into an individual's private wellbeing activity.
Benefits leaders receive evidence strong enough for renewal while preserving the confidentiality on which participation depends.
Leadership reporting shows purpose, cohort definition, minimum population, suppression, access, and export history.
Privacy confidence becomes a contract-health measure because member trust is necessary for valid employer outcomes.
The employer console exposes approved aggregate outcomes and campaigns while blocking named member activity and unsafe drill-down.
Builds renewal evidence from governed cohorts and aggregate usefulness rather than employee-level risk classification.
Enforces purpose, consent, cohort size, suppression, retention, access, and emergency exceptions at the data boundary.
Produces privacy-protected program measures with visible cohort and suppression rules and no individual reconstruction path.
Keeps employer eligibility and administration separate from the member's private participation identity.
Owns a contract and reporting model that protects members while giving employers useful program-level decisions.
Makes provable employer value without employee surveillance a core enterprise wellbeing benchmark.

stressors.name: A regional crisis triples requests for help while local professional support capacity collapses
stressors.detection: Member intent and urgency signals, moderation queues, live-session demand, referral acceptance, provider availability, regional resource status, wait times, contributor capacity, and public emergency information.
stressors.attractor: Many members arrive with urgent and changing needs while familiar sessions, contributors, and external providers are full or unavailable. A simple recommendation loop keeps sending people toward scarce options, overloads moderators, creates silent waits, and blurs the line between community support and care that requires qualified professionals.
stressors.businessReaction: Publish clear service boundaries and wait expectations, prioritize safe human review, expand moderated group and asynchronous support where appropriate, continuously verify external resources and capacity, offer members realistic choices, and follow through until a referral is accepted or another safe path is chosen.
stressors.residue: Separate member need, urgency indicator, consent, location, language, support scope, support option, provider or contributor, capacity window, queue position, referral, acceptance, follow-up, and escalation. Routing uses current capacity and scope rather than a static directory; community support can absorb suitable demand while higher-consequence cases retain human oversight and documented handoff.

impacts.effect: Contributors help more people during a surge without being pushed beyond their role, competence, or safe capacity.
Members can move from self-guided support to an available higher-touch option when circumstances change.
Escalation shows current capacity, safe interim options, consent, handoff status, and what happens next.
Time to meaningful support measures arrival at a suitable available interaction, not a click on a full provider listing.
Adds capacity-aware choices, transparent waits, moderated interim support, referral acceptance, and follow-up state.
Coordinates consent, urgency review, support scope, current capacity, handoff, and follow-up during a demand surge.
Matches against verified scope and live capacity and preserves the member's choices and handoff status.
Versions regional availability, eligibility, languages, service boundary, wait, and last verification.
Prioritizes human queues, distributes work safely, and links community events to referral and follow-up.
Owns surge response across moderation, contributors, member communication, external resources, and referral follow-through.
Makes safe capacity-aware navigation from digital wellbeing to appropriate outside support a market benchmark.

stressors.name: After a workplace tragedy, an employer asks who is at risk and requests immediate targeted outreach
stressors.detection: Employer incident notice, affected locations and eligibility cohorts, voluntary member requests, aggregate demand, moderation and referral queues, verified regional resources, support capacity, consent, and employer access logs.
stressors.attractor: Leadership urgently wants to protect employees and asks for names, scores, and outreach based on private activity. At the same time, automated recommendations face stronger oversight and relevant community, contributor, and external care capacity is constrained. Either doing nothing or exposing individuals creates serious harm.
stressors.businessReaction: Launch an employer-funded response for the affected cohort without identifying private participants, communicate voluntary support options directly to eligible members, explain support scope, triage only through governed member-facing processes, scale moderated and external capacity, and report aggregate reach, waits, and service quality back to the employer.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: recommendation evidence and scope prevent an opaque automated risk list, employer-member separation blocks named activity disclosure, and the capacity-aware escalation model supports voluntary outreach, current resource choices, human review, and follow-up. The existing parts combine into one governed incident program.

impacts.effect: HR can operate a rapid workforce response while preserving the confidentiality and voluntary participation that make it trustworthy.
Program administrators adapt support to an acute workforce need using governed aggregate demand rather than named risk scores.
The incident report explains cohort outreach, voluntary use, capacity, service quality, privacy controls, and unresolved needs.
Program tuning now includes how quickly safe capacity and relevant programming adapt without compromising member confidentiality.
Composes an affected cohort, approved communications, aggregate response, capacity status, and stewardship evidence without member identities.
Reuses launch mechanics for a time-bound incident program with privacy, scope, capacity, and follow-up controls already attached.
Lets an employer fund, communicate, and monitor the incident response while exposing only permitted aggregate state.
Applies existing purpose, separation, cohort, suppression, consent, access, and emergency-process rules.
Uses the existing scope- and capacity-aware referral flow for members who voluntarily request higher-touch support.
Coordinates the employer response with trust, community care, contributors, member communication, and external providers.
Makes privacy-preserving crisis response and defensible employer reporting an enterprise wellbeing benchmark.
